claim: Disrupted sleep is a major feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), often arising years before symptoms of cognitive decline.
source: Disrupted sleep is a major feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), often arising years before symptoms of cognitive decline.
evidence: This is a general statement about AD and sleep disruption that is part of established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Prolonged wakefulness exacerbates the production of amyloid-beta (Aβ) species.
source: Prolonged wakefulness exacerbates the production of amyloid-beta (Aβ) species, a major driver of AD progression, suggesting that sleep loss further accelerates AD through a vicious cycle.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about the relationship between wakefulness and Aβ production.

claim: Aβ acutely and reversibly enhances or suppresses sleep as a function of oligomer length in zebrafish.
source: We demonstrate in zebrafish that Aβ acutely and reversibly enhances or suppresses sleep as a function of oligomer length.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Short Aβ oligomers induce acute wakefulness through Adrenergic receptor b2 (Adrb2) and Progesterone membrane receptor component 1 (Pgrmc1).
source: Genetic disruptions revealed that short Aβ oligomers induce acute wakefulness through Adrenergic receptor b2 (Adrb2) and Progesterone membrane receptor component 1 (Pgrmc1), while longer Aβ forms induce sleep through a pharmacologically tractable Prion Protein (PrP) signaling cascade.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic disruption experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Longer Aβ forms induce sleep through a pharmacologically tractable Prion Protein (PrP) signaling cascade.
source: Genetic disruptions revealed that short Aβ oligomers induce acute wakefulness through Adrenergic receptor b2 (Adrb2) and Progesterone membrane receptor component 1 (Pgrmc1), while longer Aβ forms induce sleep through a pharmacologically tractable Prion Protein (PrP) signaling cascade.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic and pharmacological experiments shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Change in Aβ levels in the brain is one of the earliest known pathological events in AD and is detectable years before the development of Aβ plaques and decades before the clinical onset of AD.
source: Change in Aβ levels in the brain is one of the earliest known pathological events in AD and is detectable years before the development of Aβ plaques and decades before the clinical onset of AD (Bateman et al., 2007; Jack et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Aβ is an ancient neuropeptide conserved across vertebrates through at least 400 million years of evolution.
source: However, Aβ is an ancient neuropeptide conserved across vertebrates through at least 400 million years of evolution (Moir and Tanzi, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Aβ's cleavage from amyloid precursor protein (APP) is tightly regulated by multiple enzymatic reactions.
source: Aβ's cleavage from amyloid precursor protein (APP) is tightly regulated by multiple enzymatic reactions (O'Brien and Wong, 2011), and its release from neurons is carefully controlled (Kamenetz et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Aβ release from neurons is carefully controlled.
source: Aβ's cleavage from amyloid precursor protein (APP) is tightly regulated by multiple enzymatic reactions (O'Brien and Wong, 2011), and its release from neurons is carefully controlled (Kamenetz et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Aβ interacts with numerous surface receptors and can activate intrinsic cellular signalling cascades to alter neuronal and synaptic function.
source: Aβ interacts with numerous surface receptors and can activate intrinsic cellular signalling cascades to alter neuronal and synaptic function (Jarosz-Griffiths et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Aβ has been suggested to act as an antimicrobial peptide.
source: More recently, Aβ has been suggested to act as an antimicrobial peptide (Soscia et al., 2010), and the deposition of Aβ may be induced as an innate immune defence mechanism against microbial pathogens (Kumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The deposition of Aβ may be induced as an innate immune defence mechanism against microbial pathogens.
source: More recently, Aβ has been suggested to act as an antimicrobial peptide (Soscia et al., 2010), and the deposition of Aβ may be induced as an innate immune defence mechanism against microbial pathogens (Kumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: AD patients have sleep-wake abnormalities, including insomnia at night and increased napping during the day.
source: One of the earliest symptoms of AD is the disruption of sleep, and AD patients have sleep-wake abnormalities, including insomnia at night and increased napping during the day (Allen et al., 1987; Loewenstein et al., 1982; Moran et al., 2005; Prinz et al., 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Multiple transgenic AD mouse models that overproduce Aβ show disrupted sleep phenotypes.
source: Multiple transgenic AD mouse models that overproduce Aβ also show disrupted sleep phenotypes (Roh et al., 2012; Sterniczuk et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2002), often in the absence of neuronal loss and preceding impairments of learning and memory (Irizarry et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Disrupted sleep phenotypes in transgenic AD mouse models often occur in the absence of neuronal loss and precede impairments of learning and memory.
source: Multiple transgenic AD mouse models that overproduce Aβ also show disrupted sleep phenotypes (Roh et al., 2012; Sterniczuk et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2002), often in the absence of neuronal loss and preceding impairments of learning and memory (Irizarry et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Aβ levels in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are modulated by the sleep-wake cycle in non-pathological conditions.
source: In non-pathological conditions, Aβ levels in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) are modulated by the sleep-wake cycle (Kang et al., 2009; Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Aβ generation and release are controlled by electrical and synaptic activity.
source: Aβ generation and release are controlled by electrical and synaptic activity (Cirrito et al., 2005; Kamenetz et al., 2003), leading to increased extracellular Aβ levels during wakefulness and decreased levels during sleep (Kang et al., 2009; Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Extracellular Aβ levels increase during wakefulness and decrease during sleep.
source: Aβ generation and release are controlled by electrical and synaptic activity (Cirrito et al., 2005; Kamenetz et al., 2003), leading to increased extracellular Aβ levels during wakefulness and decreased levels during sleep (Kang et al., 2009; Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Heart-injected fluorescently-tagged Aβ42 penetrates the whole larval zebrafish brain within 1-3 hours post-injection.
source: This technique rapidly (<1 hr, peaking within 2–3 hr) and reversibly delivers Aβ to the larval brain, as assessed by injection of fluorescently tagged Aβ42 and subsequent confocal brain imaging (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Aβ42 incubated overnight at 4°C consists of shorter oligomers (mean 45 ± 11 nm, median = 39 nm) than when incubated at 25°C (mean 75 ± 10 nm, median = 61 nm) or at 37°C (mean 121 ± 10 nm, median = 88 nm).
source: Aβ42 incubated overnight at 4°C consisted of fewer and shorter oligomers (Aβshort, mean 45 ± 11 nm, median = 39 nm) than when incubated at 25°C (Aβlong, mean 75 ± 10 nm, median = 61 nm) or at 37°C (Aβv-long, mean 121 ± 10 nm, median = 88 nm) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Aβshort significantly increased waking activity by +12.8% relative to Aβrev.
source: In the day following injection, Aβshort significantly increased waking activity by +12.8% and reduced total sleep relative to Aβrev by 15.5% (Figure 1D–E').
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D-E'.

claim: Aβshort reduced total sleep relative to Aβrev by 15.5%.
source: In the day following injection, Aβshort significantly increased waking activity by +12.8% and reduced total sleep relative to Aβrev by 15.5% (Figure 1D–E').
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D-E'.

claim: The effects of Aβshort on sleep and waking activity were reversible, with no significant differences between Aβshort and reverse peptide in the night following injection.
source: These effects were reversible, as there were no significant differences in sleep (Figure 1E, black bar) or waking activity (Figure 1D, black bar) between Aβshort and reverse peptide in the night following injection, and the behavior of Aβshort-injected larvae returned to baseline levels in the subsequent day (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D, 1E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Injection of Aβlong significantly increased sleep during the post-injection day by +47.2%.
source: In contrast, while injection of longer Aβ fibers (Aβv_long) had no effect on behavior, (Figure 1H–I'), injection of the intermediate Aβlong oligomers significantly increased sleep during the post-injection day by +47.2% and reduced waking activity by 11.3% (Figure 1F–G').
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1F-G'.

claim: Injection of Aβlong reduced waking activity by 11.3%.
source: In contrast, while injection of longer Aβ fibers (Aβv_long) had no effect on behavior, (Figure 1H–I'), injection of the intermediate Aβlong oligomers significantly increased sleep during the post-injection day by +47.2% and reduced waking activity by 11.3% (Figure 1F–G').
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1F-G'.

claim: The increased sleep induced by Aβlong was due to a significant increase in the average number of sleep bouts but not an increase in sleep bout length.
source: The increased sleep induced by Aβlong was due to a significant increase in the average number of sleep bouts but not an increase in sleep bout length (Figure 1J), indicating higher sleep initiation is responsible for the change in sleep rather than an increased sleep consolidation.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Injection with either long or short forms of Aβ had no effect on apoptosis, as detected by staining for activation of Caspase-3.
source: First, injection with either long or short forms of Aβ had no effect on apoptosis, as detected by staining for activation of Caspase-3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Caspase-3 staining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Aβ injected animals raised to adulthood showed no major differences in their general health or in their survival rates.
source: In addition, Aβ injected animals raised to adulthood showed no major differences in their general health or in their survival rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Aβshort upregulated c-fos expression in several discrete areas of the larval brain including the posterior hypothalamus and the dorsal and ventral telencephalon.
source: In situ hybridization (ISH) for expression of the immediate early gene, c-fos, identified several discrete areas of the larval brain that are upregulated after injection of Aβshort relative to Aβrev, including the posterior hypothalamus and the dorsal and ventral telencephalon (Figure 2A), areas that are also upregulated in mutants with extended wakefulness (Ashlin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: c-fos expression following Aβlong injections was globally dampened relative to Aβrev.
source: In contrast, c-fos expression following Aβlong injections was globally dampened relative to Aβrev (Figure 2B) in a manner consistent with the low expression of c-fos in WT brains collected at ZT19, when larvae are maximally asleep (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Aβshort upregulated P-ERK in the ventral telencephalon and posterior hypothalamus.
source: Consistent with c-fos induction, Aβshort upregulated P-ERK in the ventral telencephalon and posterior hypothalamus (Figure 2D and D', Figure 2—source data 1), while Aβlong resulted in a widespread reduction in p-ERK levels throughout most of the brain (Figure 2E and E', Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by pERK/tERK mapping data shown in Figure 2D and D'.

claim: Aβlong resulted in a widespread reduction in p-ERK levels throughout most of the brain.
source: Consistent with c-fos induction, Aβshort upregulated P-ERK in the ventral telencephalon and posterior hypothalamus (Figure 2D and D', Figure 2—source data 1), while Aβlong resulted in a widespread reduction in p-ERK levels throughout most of the brain (Figure 2E and E', Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by pERK/tERK mapping data shown in Figure 2E and E'.

claim: Wake-promoting Aβshort slightly decreased the number of galanin-positive cells in the hypothalamus by 6%.
source: Similarly, ISH for galanin 4–6 hr post-injection of Aβ oligomers revealed that wake-promoting Aβshort slightly decreased (−6%, blinded counts), while sleep-promoting Aβlong slightly increased (+12%, blinded counts), the number of galanin-positive cells in the hypothalamus compared to Aβrev injected larvae (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: Sleep-promoting Aβlong slightly increased the number of galanin-positive cells in the hypothalamus by 12%.
source: Similarly, ISH for galanin 4–6 hr post-injection of Aβ oligomers revealed that wake-promoting Aβshort slightly decreased (−6%, blinded counts), while sleep-promoting Aβlong slightly increased (+12%, blinded counts), the number of galanin-positive cells in the hypothalamus compared to Aβrev injected larvae (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: Neither the adrb2a-/- nor the pgrmc1-/- mutants increased waking activity in response to Aβshort injection.
source: Unlike the wild type controls, neither the adrb2a-/- nor the pgrmc1-/- mutants increased waking activity (Figure 3A–C and E) or suppressed sleep as observed in wild-type controls (Figure 3A'–C' and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A-C and E.

claim: Injection of Aβshort into adrb2a-/- animals significantly increased sleep by +83.7% instead of reducing it as in wild-type larvae.
source: Injection of Aβshort into adrb2a-/- animals even significantly increased sleep (+83.7%) instead of reducing it as in wild-type larvae (Figure 3B' and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3B' and G.

claim: Aβshort injected into prp1-/-; prp2-/- mutants elicited slightly stronger increases in waking activity and significantly large (−45%) reductions in sleep.
source: In contrast, Aβshort injected into mutants that lack both zebrafish Prp orthologs (prp1-/-; prp2-/-) elicited slightly stronger increases in waking activity and significantly large (−45%) reductions in sleep (Figure 3D,D', F and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3D, D', F and H.

claim: The wake-promoting activity of Aβshort requires intact Adrb2a and Pgrmc1 but not functional Prp1 and Prp2.
source: Thus, the wake-promoting activity of Aβshort requires intact Adrb2a and Pgrmc1 but not functional Prp1 and Prp2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: prp1-/-;prp2-/- null mutants failed to increase sleep in response to Aβlong injection compared to wild-type controls.
source: After injection of Aβlong, prp1-/-;prp2-/- null mutants failed to increase sleep compared to wild-type controls (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: The modest reduction of wakefulness induced by Aβlong was reversed in prp1-/-;prp2-/- mutants, with Aβlong instead significantly increasing wakefulness.
source: The modest reduction of wakefulness induced by Aβlong was even reversed in prp1-/-;prp2-/- mutants, with Aβlong instead significantly increasing wakefulness (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Functional Prp1 and Prp2 are essential for sleep induced by Aβlong.
source: Thus, while Prps are not required for the wake-inducing effects of Aβshort, functional Prp1 and Prp2 are essential for sleep induced by Aβlong.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Lack of either Adrb2a or Pgrmc1 abolished the neuronal activity-inducing effect of Aβshort as detected by c-fos expression.
source: Consistently, lack of either Adrb2a or Pgrmc1 abolished the neuronal activity-inducing effect of Aβshort (Figure 5A), as detected by in situ hybridization for c-fos.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Aβlong injections into the prp1-/-; prp2-/- double mutants elicited no reduction in c-fos expression.
source: Similarly, although Aβlong dampens neuronal activity when injected into wild-type larvae, Aβlong injections into the prp1-/-; prp2-/- double mutants elicited no reduction in c-fos expression (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Chicago Sky Blue 6B, a small molecule that disrupts Aβ-PrP interactions, significantly abolished the sleep-inducing effect of Aβlong.
source: Consistent with a role for direct Aβlong-Prp interactions in sleep, soaking the larvae in Chicago Sky Blue 6B, a small molecule reported to disrupt Aβ-PrP interactions (Risse et al., 2015), significantly abolished the sleep-inducing effect of Aβlong (Figure 6B and C, S7A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of mGluR5 with MPEP significantly blocked the sleep-inducing properties of Aβlong.
source: Similarly, pharmacological inhibition of either of the putative Aβ-Prp downstream signalling components Metabotropic Glutamate Receptor 5 (mGluR5) or Fyn kinase (Um et al., 2013; Um et al., 2012) significantly blocked the sleep-inducing properties of Aβlong (Figure 6D and E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Fyn kinase with saracatinib significantly blocked the sleep-inducing properties of Aβlong.
source: Similarly, pharmacological inhibition of either of the putative Aβ-Prp downstream signalling components Metabotropic Glutamate Receptor 5 (mGluR5) or Fyn kinase (Um et al., 2013; Um et al., 2012) significantly blocked the sleep-inducing properties of Aβlong (Figure 6D and E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Co-injection of both Aβshort and Aβlong resulted in an intermediate phenotype that is indistinguishable from control injections of Aβrev.
source: As expected, Aβshort alone reduced sleep and Aβlong alone increased sleep. In contrast, co-injection of both Aβshort and Aβlong resulted in an intermediate phenotype that is indistinguishable from control injections of Aβrev (Figure 6F), suggesting that the effects of Aβshort and Aβlong are additive and likely act through distinct neuronal circuits or signaling cascades to modulate sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The effects of Aβshort and Aβlong are additive and likely act through distinct neuronal circuits or signaling cascades to modulate sleep.
source: As expected, Aβshort alone reduced sleep and Aβlong alone increased sleep. In contrast, co-injection of both Aβshort and Aβlong resulted in an intermediate phenotype that is indistinguishable from control injections of Aβrev (Figure 6F), suggesting that the effects of Aβshort and Aβlong are additive and likely act through distinct neuronal circuits or signaling cascades to modulate sleep.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the co-injection experiment shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Aβ can acutely increase or decrease sleep and wake behaviors and brain states through behaviorally relevant molecular targets and independently of neuronal cell death.
source: Our results show that, depending on its oligomeric form, Aβ can acutely increase or decrease sleep and wake behaviors and brain states through behaviorally relevant molecular targets and independently of neuronal cell death.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claim: Aβ dimers have been shown to directly bind human ADRB2 with high-affinity, causing increased calcium influx and neuronal hyper-activation in rat prefrontal cortical slices.
source: For example, Aβ dimers, which have been detected in the brains of AD patients ( Vázquez de la Torre et al., 2018), have been shown to directly bind human ADRB2 with high-affinity, causing increased calcium influx and neuronal hyper-activation in rat prefrontal cortical slices (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PGRMC1 can be activated by AD brain extracts and has shown preferential binding for 50–75 kDa Aβ species in vitro.
source: PGRMC1 can be activated by AD brain extracts (Izzo et al., 2014b) and also has shown preferential binding for 50–75 kDa Aβ species in vitro (Izzo et al., 2014a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PrP has been identified as a direct binding partner for longer Aβ-oligomers of 20–200 nm in length.
source: Our results are also consistent with studies that have identified PrP as a direct binding partner (Laurén et al., 2009) for longer Aβ-oligomers of 20–200 nm in length (Nicoll et al., 2013), the size range of our sleep-inducing Aβlong preparation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In neuronal culture and slice preparations, longer Aβ-oligomers trigger reduction of synaptic strength via a Prp signaling cascade through mGluR5 and Fyn kinase activation.
source: In neuronal culture and slice preparations, longer Aβ-oligomers trigger reduction of synaptic strength (Laurén et al., 2009) via a Prp signaling cascade through mGluR5 and Fyn kinase activation (Um et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Temperature changes in the physiological range (35–42°C) have been reported to significantly affect Aβ oligomerization.
source: For example, temperature changes in the physiological range (35–42°C) have been reported to significantly affect Aβ oligomerization (Ghavami et al., 2013), suggesting that either the natural daily fluctuation in body temperature (in humans, up to 2°C) or the induction of a fever can promote changes in amyloidogenic Aβ generation (Szaruga et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The amount and type of Aβ oligomeric species found in healthy brains change across the human life cycle.
source: On longer timescales, the amount and type of Aβ oligomeric species (including dimers, cross-linked dimers, trimers, and 56 kDa oligomers) found in healthy brains change across the human life cycle (Lesné et al., 2013) and are heterogeneous and elevated in AD patients (Izzo et al., 2014a; Kostylev et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Short (dimers, trimers) Aβ oligomers are more enriched in the early, mild cognitive impairment (MCI) stages of AD, while longer oligomers predominate in the CSF at later clinical stages of AD.
source: Although the precise makeup of Aβ species present in healthy and AD brains has remained difficult to quantify (Benilova et al., 2012), some studies have indicated that short (dimers, trimers) Aβ oligomers are more enriched in the early, mild cognitive impairment (MCI) stages of AD, while longer oligomers predominate in the CSF at later clinical stages of AD (De et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: AD progression is associated with increasingly large disruptions in sleep patterns, with patients exhibiting high levels of sleep fragmentation, a lack of circadian rhythm, night-time insomnia and irregular daytime napping throughout the day.
source: Similarly, AD progression is associated with increasingly large disruptions in sleep patterns, with patients exhibiting high levels of sleep fragmentation, a lack of circadian rhythm, night-time insomnia and irregular daytime napping throughout the day (Videnovic et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Sleep symptoms of both normal aging and AD may reflect changes in Aβ burden that lead to an altered balance in sleep- and wake-promoting signaling cascades.
source: One possibility consistent with our data is that sleep symptoms of both normal aging and AD may reflect changes in Aβ burden that lead to an altered balance in sleep- and wake-promoting signaling cascades.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The estimated final concentration of injected Aβ falls within the lower range of physiological concentrations reported for Aβ42 in human CSF of 100 pM-5nM.
source: We estimate this dose yields a final concentration that falls within the lower range of physiological concentrations reported for Aβ42 in human CSF of 100 pM-5nM (Bateman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on calculations and comparison to cited physiological concentrations.

claim: Zebrafish larvae have conserved APP processing machinery and Aβ peptides.
source: To test this, we took advantage of the ability to directly deliver small molecules and Aβ peptides to the brain of larval zebrafish, which have conserved APP processing machinery and Aβ peptides (Newman et al., 2014) and share genetic, pharmacological, and neuronal sleep-regulatory mechanisms with mammals (Barlow and Rihel, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Zebrafish share genetic, pharmacological, and neuronal sleep-regulatory mechanisms with mammals.
source: To test this, we took advantage of the ability to directly deliver small molecules and Aβ peptides to the brain of larval zebrafish, which have conserved APP processing machinery and Aβ peptides (Newman et al., 2014) and share genetic, pharmacological, and neuronal sleep-regulatory mechanisms with mammals (Barlow and Rihel, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Galanin-expressing neurons of the preoptic area and hypothalamus are active and upregulate galanin transcription during zebrafish sleep.
source: Galanin-expressing neurons of the preoptic area and hypothalamus are active and upregulate galanin transcription during zebrafish sleep (Reichert et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Aβ dimers have been detected in the brains of AD patients.
source: For example, Aβ dimers, which have been detected in the brains of AD patients ( Vázquez de la Torre et al., 2018), have been shown to directly bind human ADRB2 with high-affinity, causing increased calcium influx and neuronal hyper-activation in rat prefrontal cortical slices (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Aβ burden is acutely increased by sleep deprivation.
source: As Aβ burden is acutely increased by sleep deprivation (Shokri-Kojori et al., 2018), perturbations to the normal sleep-wake cycle may feedback on behavior through altered Aβ signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Microbial infection can trigger Aβ fibrilization.
source: In addition, Aβ can act as an antimicrobial peptide (Kumar et al., 2016; Soscia et al., 2010), and microbial infection can trigger Aβ fibrilization (Eimer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Infection and fever are potent drivers of sleep.
source: Considering that infection and fever are also potent drivers of sleep (Imeri and Opp, 2009), the sleep-inducing Aβ-Prp signaling pathway we identified here could mediate recovery sleep during illness-- a hypothesis for future investigation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The sleep-inducing Aβ-Prp signaling pathway could mediate recovery sleep during illness.
source: Considering that infection and fever are also potent drivers of sleep (Imeri and Opp, 2009), the sleep-inducing Aβ-Prp signaling pathway we identified here could mediate recovery sleep during illness-- a hypothesis for future investigation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The elimination of either Adrb2a or Pgrmc1 is sufficient to fully prevent Aβshort-induced wakefulness.
source: For example, the elimination of either Adrb2a or Pgrmc1 is sufficient to fully prevent Aβshort-induced wakefulness.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Adrb2a and Pgrmc1 function in the same molecular pathway for Aβshort-induced wakefulness.
source: This suggests that Adrb2a and Pgrmc1 function in the same molecular pathway, and signaling by Aβ on either alone is insufficient to modulate behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the genetic data.

claim: At least one study has suggested that Adrb2a and Pgrmc1 can directly physically interact.
source: Not much is known about how these two receptors interact with one another, but at least one study (Roy et al., 2013) has suggested they can directly physically interact.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Adrb2a, Pgrmc1, and Prp receptors have widespread expression in zebrafish.
source: It also remains unclear if the Aβshort-Adrb2a/Pgrmc1 wake pathway and the Aβlong-Prp sleep pathway occur in the same or different sets of neurons to modulate behavior, as these receptors have widespread expression in zebrafish (Cotto et al., 2005; Málaga-Trillo et al., 2009; Steele et al., 2011; Thisse and Thisse, 2004; Wang et al., 2009), although our co-injection experiment suggests they act on parallel neuronal circuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The co-injection experiment suggests that Aβshort-Adrb2a/Pgrmc1 wake pathway and the Aβlong-Prp sleep pathway act on parallel neuronal circuits.
source: It also remains unclear if the Aβshort-Adrb2a/Pgrmc1 wake pathway and the Aβlong-Prp sleep pathway occur in the same or different sets of neurons to modulate behavior, as these receptors have widespread expression in zebrafish (Cotto et al., 2005; Málaga-Trillo et al., 2009; Steele et al., 2011; Thisse and Thisse, 2004; Wang et al., 2009), although our co-injection experiment suggests they act on parallel neuronal circuits.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the co-injection experiment.

claim: Numerous wake- and sleep-promoting neuronal populations have been uncovered in zebrafish.
source: Numerous wake- and sleep-promoting neuronal populations that could serve as neuronal targets for these signalling cascades to drive changes in behavioral state have been uncovered in zebrafish (Barlow and Rihel, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Alterations to the ratio of Aβ oligomeric forms present in the brain could have differential effects on sleep-wake regulation.
source: However, our model predicts that alterations to the ratio of Aβ oligomeric forms present in the brain could have differential effects on sleep-wake regulation, as the balance between sleep- and wake- promoting Aβ signals is tilted to favour one pathway over the other (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the study's findings.

claim: Changes in extracellular Aβ levels could sculpt behavior over the normal 24 hr circadian cycle.
source: Given the natural daily increase in Aβ secretion during wakefulness and increased levels of Aβ clearance during sleep (Xie et al., 2013), changes in extracellular Aβ levels could sculpt behavior over the normal 24 hr circadian cycle.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on known Aβ dynamics and the study's findings.

claim: Perturbations to the normal sleep-wake cycle may feedback on behavior through altered Aβ signaling.
source: As Aβ burden is acutely increased by sleep deprivation (Shokri-Kojori et al., 2018), perturbations to the normal sleep-wake cycle may feedback on behavior through altered Aβ signaling.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on cited research and the study's findings.

claim: The natural daily fluctuation in body temperature (in humans, up to 2°C) or the induction of a fever can promote changes in amyloidogenic Aβ generation.
source: For example, temperature changes in the physiological range (35–42°C) have been reported to significantly affect Aβ oligomerization (Ghavami et al., 2013), suggesting that either the natural daily fluctuation in body temperature (in humans, up to 2°C) or the induction of a fever can promote changes in amyloidogenic Aβ generation (Szaruga et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited research about temperature effects on Aβ.

claim: Aβ oligomeric species are heterogeneous and elevated in AD patients.
source: On longer timescales, the amount and type of Aβ oligomeric species (including dimers, cross-linked dimers, trimers, and 56 kDa oligomers) found in healthy brains change across the human life cycle (Lesné et al., 2013) and are heterogeneous and elevated in AD patients (Izzo et al., 2014a; Kostylev et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: These signaling molecules might be potential therapeutic targets for treating disrupted sleep early in AD progression, which may in turn slow disease progression.
source: These signaling molecules might therefore be potential therapeutic targets for treating disrupted sleep early in AD progression, which may in turn slow disease progression.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: The intra-cardiac injection assay in 5 days post fertilization (5 dpf) larval zebrafish avoids direct damage to brain tissue.
source: Our minimally invasive intra-cardiac injection assay in 5 days post fertilization (5 dpf) larval zebrafish avoids direct damage to brain tissue (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: The injection technique rapidly (<1 hr, peaking within 2–3 hr) and reversibly delivers Aβ to the larval brain.
source: This technique rapidly (<1 hr, peaking within 2–3 hr) and reversibly delivers Aβ to the larval brain, as assessed by injection of fluorescently tagged Aβ42 and subsequent confocal brain imaging (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Aβ42 incubated overnight at increasing temperatures generates Aβ oligomeric pools with significantly different lengths.
source: By incubating Aβ42 overnight at increasing temperatures, we generated Aβ oligomeric pools with significantly different lengths, as measured by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Injection of longer Aβ fibers (Aβv_long) had no effect on behavior.
source: In contrast, while injection of longer Aβ fibers (Aβv_long) had no effect on behavior, (Figure 1H–I'), injection of the intermediate Aβlong oligomers significantly increased sleep during the post-injection day by +47.2% and reduced waking activity by 11.3% (Figure 1F–G').
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1H-I'.

claim: Larvae undergoing no treatment, anesthesia only, mock injection, or PBS only injections had indistinguishable effects on sleep/wake.
source: Additional control experiments ruled out experimental artefacts, as larvae undergoing no treatment, anesthesia only, mock injection, or PBS only injections had indistinguishable effects on sleep/wake (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H-J.

claim: Both Aβshort and Aβlong injected larvae responded normally to salient stimuli such as a light:dark pulse.
source: Second, both Aβshort and Aβlong injected larvae responded normally to salient stimuli such as a light:dark pulse, demonstrating that these larvae were not paralyzed, in a coma, or undergoing sickness behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The bout structure of Aβrev, Aβshort, and Aβlong injected fish was highly similar to WT behavior.
source: The bout structure of Aβrev, Aβshort, and Aβlong injected fish was highly similar to WT behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E and Figure 1—video 1), and the high-frequency bouts (HFB) indicative of seizures (Reichert et al., 2019) were only found in PTZ exposed fish but not Aβ injected larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E.

claim: High-frequency bouts (HFB) indicative of seizures were only found in PTZ exposed fish but not Aβ injected larvae.
source: The bout structure of Aβrev, Aβshort, and Aβlong injected fish was highly similar to WT behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E and Figure 1—video 1), and the high-frequency bouts (HFB) indicative of seizures (Reichert et al., 2019) were only found in PTZ exposed fish but not Aβ injected larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E.

claim: The changes in behavior after Aβ exposure are due to acute signalling events.
source: Together these experiments indicate that exposure to Aβ modulates normal sleep/wake behavior without inducing toxic states. We conclude that the changes in behavior after Aβ exposure are due to acute signalling events and therefore sought to identify the neuronal and molecular substrates through which Aβ signals to modulate sleep/wake behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control experiments.

claim: The c-fos patterns induced by Aβshort match at least nine populations of c-fos-positive neurons in waking WT brains collected at ZT1.
source: Comparing the Aβshort induced c-fos patterns to WT brains collected at zeitgeber time 1 (ZT1, ZT0 = lights ON), when larvae are maximally awake, reveals at least nine populations of c-fos-positive neurons in both Aβshort and waking brains (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: c-fos expression in WT brains is low at ZT19, when larvae are maximally asleep.
source: In contrast, c-fos expression following Aβlong injections was globally dampened relative to Aβrev (Figure 2B) in a manner consistent with the low expression of c-fos in WT brains collected at ZT19, when larvae are maximally asleep (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The neuronal activity observed in the posterior hypothalamus and the dorsal and ventral telencephalon after Aβshort into WT controls was not detected after injection into either adrb2a-/- or pgrmc1-/- mutants.
source: In particular, the neuronal activity observed in the posterior hypothalamus and the dorsal and ventral telencephalon after Aβshort into WT controls was not detected after injection into either adrb2a-/- or pgrmc1-/- mutants (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: c-fos expression in the telencephalon and hypothalamus was upregulated in prp1-/-; prp2-/- double mutants after Aβlong injection relative to reverse injected controls.
source: Instead, c-fos expression in the telencephalon and hypothalamus was upregulated relative to reverse injected controls (Figure 5B), consistent with the increased behavioral wakefulness observed in the prp mutants (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Aβshort acutely upregulates neuronal activity and behavioral wakefulness through interactions with Adrb2a and Pgrmc1.
source: Together, these data are consistent with Aβshort acutely upregulating neuronal activity and behavioral wakefulness through interactions with Adrb2a and Pgrmc1, while Aβlong interactions with Prp drive increased sleep and a global reduction in neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic and neuronal activity data.

claim: Aβlong interactions with Prp drive increased sleep and a global reduction in neuronal activity.
source: Together, these data are consistent with Aβshort acutely upregulating neuronal activity and behavioral wakefulness through interactions with Adrb2a and Pgrmc1, while Aβlong interactions with Prp drive increased sleep and a global reduction in neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic and neuronal activity data.

claim: Both genetic and pharmacological interference with several steps of the Aβ-Prp-mGluR5-Fyn kinase signaling cascade prevents the ability of Aβlong to increase sleep behavior.
source: Thus, both genetic and pharmacological interference with several steps of the Aβ-Prp-mGluR5-Fyn kinase signaling cascade prevents the ability of Aβlong to increase sleep behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic and pharmacological experiments.

claim: The bi-directional Aβ modulation of sleep and wakefulness predicts that alterations to the relative concentrations of different Aβ oligomeric forms during healthy aging and AD disease progression will have opposing consequences on sleep and wake behavior.
source: However, the bi-directional Aβ modulation of sleep and wakefulness (Figure 6G) predicts that alterations to the relative concentrations of different Aβ oligomeric forms during healthy aging and AD disease progression will have opposing consequences on sleep and wake behavior.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the study's findings.

claim: adrb2a-/- mutants have increased sleep during the day compared to wild type and heterozygous siblings.
source: Except for a mild increase in daytime sleep in adrb2a-/- mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D'–F'), none of these mutants exhibited changes in baseline sleep and wake on a 14 hr:10 hr light:dark cycle as compared to wild type and heterozygous siblings (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–F'; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–F').
evidence: This claim is supported by baseline behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D'-F'.

claim: prp1-/-;prp2-/- double mutants have no significant differences in day or night sleep and waking activity compared to prp+/+ siblings under baseline conditions.
source: Under baseline conditions, we also detected no significant differences in day or night sleep and waking activity in prp1-/-;prp2-/- double mutants compared to prp+/+ siblings generated from either prp1+/-; prp2+/- or prp1+/-;prp2-/- in-crosses (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–F').
evidence: This claim is supported by baseline behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-F'.

claim: The sleep-inducing Prp pathway is likely co-activated along with the wake-promoting pathway by Aβ to partially dampen the behavioral response of wild-type larvae.
source: Moreover, since prp double mutants have exacerbated wakefulness in response to Aβshort injections, the sleep-inducing Prp pathway is likely co-activated along with the wake-promoting pathway by Aβ to partially dampen the behavioral response of wild-type larvae (Figure 3D and H).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enhanced wakefulness response in prp mutants.

claim: The mGluR5 inhibitor MPEP resulted in significant sleep reductions after exposure to Aβlong.
source: Both the mGluR5 inhibitor MPEP and the Src-kinase inhibitor saracatinib even resulted in significant sleep reductions after exposure to Aβlong.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The Src-kinase inhibitor saracatinib resulted in significant sleep reductions after exposure to Aβlong.
source: Both the mGluR5 inhibitor MPEP and the Src-kinase inhibitor saracatinib even resulted in significant sleep reductions after exposure to Aβlong.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 6E.
